read: full: abstract, sections 1-7, limitations (p.1-9); appendices A (error analysis), B (benchmark details), C (framework), D (results tables), E (human study), F.3.8 (final-answer prompt) and G (cost) read; the other prompt templates in F and the D.3-D.4 case studies skimmed.
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2606.10833v1 [cs.AI], 9 June 2026 (p.1 margin stamp); no venue shown.
what_it_is: EngVQA is a static multimodal benchmark of 696 diagram-based problems in five mechanical-engineering subjects, extracted semi-automatically from question PDFs with their solutions and manually verified against the reference material (p.3, p.6). Its evaluator, EngJudge, makes the model write its solution in eight tagged stages (problem characterization, assumptions, visual interpretation, equation selection, logical reasoning, algebraic accuracy, physical interpretation, final answer), scores each stage with a separate LLM-judge prompt using penalties and fatal-error caps, propagates upstream scores through a dependency graph, and applies verbosity, coverage and sanity meta-checks to give a 0-10 score (p.4-6). Two generator VLMs are evaluated (Qwen3-VL-8B, Gemini-2.5-Flash) with Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview as the main judge and Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct as a second (p.6); no generator reaches a mean of 4 in any subject (p.7). A study with 9 students on 4 problems each reports Pearson 0.975 against EngJudge, but the 'human' scores are EngJudge's own scores adjusted by at most 2 points after the rater had seen them (p.8, p.23).
domain: engineering (mechanical): dynamics, thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, heat and mass transfer, mechanics of materials; multimodal (technical diagrams)
size: 696 problems: Dynamics 171, Thermodynamics 236, Fluid Mechanics 93, Heat and Mass Transfer 96, Mechanics of Materials 100 (Table 2, p.3). Two generator models and two judge models (p.6).
source_of_items: existing problems and solutions extracted from 'question PDFs' (Adobe PDF Extract, PyMuPDF, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite) and manually verified against the reference material (p.6); described as 'authentic' and 'standard academic engineering physics problems' (p.2, p.9). The source books are not named.
has_gold_traces: partial: each problem has a reference solution from the source material, which the judge receives (the final-answer prompt compares against a 'GROUND TRUTH IMAGE', p.42-43); there are no stage-level gold values, and the stages are defined by the prompted output format, not by annotated gold steps (p.4-5).
evaluation: step-level or process, by LLM judge: eight stage scores from separate LLM-judge calls with penalty severities 2/4/7/10 and fatal-error caps, dependency propagation, missing-stage penalties and three meta-checks, 11 judge calls per solution (p.5-6, p.9). The final-answer stage is also judged by the LLM, which is told to compute relative error against the reference (no penalty at or below 5%, moderate to 10%, major above) (p.5, p.42-43). No deterministic check.
human_validation: Items: questions, diagrams and solutions 'manually verified against the reference material' (p.6); no counts or agreement reported. Evaluator: 9 undergraduate or graduate students, 4 randomly assigned problems each, all with Gemini 2.5 Flash solutions (p.8, p.23). Raters first marked each step correct or incorrect blind, but no agreement figure is reported for those blind ratings. They then saw EngJudge's score and justification and chose a 5-point Likert adjustment; the 'human score' is reconstructed as EngJudge's score plus delta in {-2,...,+2}, clipped to 0-10 (p.23). Pearson 0.975 and MAE 0.67 are computed on these 393 data points (285 stage, 108 meta-check) (p.23, Table 11), which the paper's own Figure 11 calls 'synthetic human scores' (p.24). 48.9% of points were rated 'About right' (p.25). The two judges are compared only through mean scores, which differ severalfold (Gemini 2.5 Flash: 2.869 by Gemini-3.1-Pro against 0.945 by Qwen3-VL-32B under EngJudge; Table 8, p.20).
contamination_measures: none: the paper says it 'cannot fully rule out benchmark contamination' and argues that multimodal multi-step problems make memorisation insufficient (p.9).

engtrace_use.explanation: Candidate; the May paper does not cite it, and EngVQA does not cite EngTrace (it cites EngiBench and EEE-Bench, p.1-2). It bears directly on the May claims that 'no existing benchmark verifies this process' (Introduction) and that engineering benchmarks 'remain limited to outcome matching' (Related Work): EngVQA scores intermediate stages of engineering solutions (p.4-6).

suggested_wording: EngVQA (Wasiq et al., 2026) scores eight stages of solutions to 696 diagram-based mechanical-engineering problems, but every stage, including the final answer, is graded by an LLM judge against a fixed reference solution, and its human check rates the judge's own scores rather than grading independently.
facts_to_cite: 696 multimodal problems with technical diagrams across five subjects: dynamics, thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, heat and mass transfer, mechanics of materials (p.1, Table 2 p.3)
Problems and solutions extracted from existing question PDFs and manually verified against the reference material (p.6)
Solutions are written in eight tagged stages, each scored 0-10 by a separate LLM-judge prompt with severity penalties and fatal-error caps, then propagated through a dependency graph (p.4-6)
The final-answer stage is also judged by the LLM against the reference, with a 5% relative-error band for full credit (p.5, p.42-43)
Two generators evaluated (Qwen3-VL-8B, Gemini-2.5-Flash), judged by Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview and Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct (p.6); no generator exceeds a mean of 4 of 10 in any subject under EngJudge (p.7)
A single-pass judge gives Gemini-2.5-Flash 8.001 where EngJudge gives 2.869 (p.7)

Evaluator validation: 9 students rated EngJudge's scores on 4 problems each; Pearson 0.975 and MAE 0.67 are computed against EngJudge's score adjusted by a Likert rating of at most +/-2 made after seeing it (p.8, p.23)
Contamination is acknowledged as not ruled out (p.9)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: engineering domain (subjects overlapping EngTrace's mechanical branch and its thermodynamics and transport domains); the argument that final-answer scoring hides reasoning failures (p.1, p.3); stage-level evaluation of intermediate reasoning (p.4-6); an attempt to validate the evaluator against humans (p.8). Lacks: generated instances (696 fixed problems, contamination not addressed, p.9); gold intermediate values (only a reference solution handed to the judge, p.42-43); any deterministic check (every stage, including the final answer's tolerance band, is judged by an LLM); independent expert validation of the evaluator (the 0.975 is anchored on EngJudge's own score, from 9 students on 4 problems of one generator, p.23). It also differs in being multimodal and single-branch, and in evaluating two models. What EngTrace adds beyond it: answers and milestones computed by template code and checked deterministically across five branches, generated instances from a private seed, and a residual judge whose step and milestone verdicts were compared with independent labels from 15 experts.
notes: (1) The headline human agreement (Pearson 0.975, MAE 0.67; abstract p.1) is not an independent grading: the 'human score' is EngJudge's score plus a Likert adjustment of at most 2 points chosen after seeing it (p.23), so a high correlation follows from the construction. The batch note and the web search note ('Pearson 0.975 against 9 students' grades') repeat the figure without this caveat; the revised text should not set it beside EngTrace's expert agreement as a like-for-like validation. (2) The abstract says 'multiple state-of-the-art open and closed source VLMs' (p.1) but two generators are evaluated (p.6). (3) Small inconsistencies: 66.7% preference for dependency scoring in the text (p.8) against 63.6% in Figure 13 (p.25); 22.3% 'average' (p.8) is 2 of 9. (4) The two judges' EngJudge scores differ severalfold for the same solutions (Table 8, p.20) and no inter-judge agreement is reported. (5) The 'stage' structure is imposed on the model's output by the prompt, so it is a rubric decomposition, not gold-step supervision.
